newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hongkong Bank sees HK economy rebounding in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Hongkong Bank sees HK economy rebounding in 1997.

text.p: Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp Ltd said on Monday it was optimistic on the economic outlook for Hong Kong next year, forecasting real GDP growth of 5.2 percent against an expected 4.6 percent this year.

George Leung, Hongkong Bank's economic adviser, said the local economy was just beginning the expansion phase of the business cycle and growth should pick up throughout 1997, powered mainly by a rebound in consumption.

"The rise in domestic consumption since the middle of this year looks set to continue into 1997, supported by the positive wealth effect generated by the prosperous local stock and property markets," he said.
Greater spending by tourists was also expected, with more visitors expected ahead of the British colony's historic reversion to Chinese sovereignty next year, Leung told Reuters.
But greater spending, along with a tighter labour market, was likely to boost inflation to 6.8 percent from 1996's forecast 6.0 percent, the bank's Economic Research Unit said.

Hongkong Bank said the territory became mired in uncharacteristically sluggish economic growth after interest rates climbed in 1994, cutting into consumer spending and deflating the stock and property markets.
But growth began picking up in the middle of this year.
"We hit the trough or bottom of the cycle in the first quarter of 1996 when GDP growth fell to 3.1 percent," Leung said, adding that momentum has been building throughout the year.
"We have seen a pick-up in retail sales figures and a rise in property and stock prices," he said, adding he expected greater consumer spending to follow as investors felt wealthier.
The government last month said September retail sales rose three percent in real terms on the year, compared with growth of one percent or less in the middle of the year.

The stock and property markets are also booming, with the blue chip Hang Seng stock index up 28 percent so far this year and mass market flat prices rising around 20 percent, according to analysts' estimates.
A more active property market was also expected to boost construction activity and help sustain capital investment in addition to ongoing infrastructure projects, the bank said.
But the bank's Economic Research Unit said the recovery of Hong Kong's external sector was expected to be slow.

An expected recovery in global demand, underpinned by stronger growth prospects in industrialised economies, will be a favourable factor in Hong Kong's external trade picture, with help from stronger import demand from China, it said.
But Leung cautioned the overall impetus for trade growth was likely to be mild in 1997.
An increasing proportion of China's exports was likely to be shipped from southern Chinese ports rather than through Hong Kong, which could affect the territory's re-export growth, he said.
External factors also underpinned the GDP forecast.
"Our forecast is based on two important factors -- 10 percent GDP growth in China in 1997 and steady interest rates in the United States and Hong Kong," Leung said.

The Economic Research Unit based its forecast on a 25 basis point rise in the U.S. and Hong Kong interest rates by the end of 1997, and Leung stressed there was no strong evidence that a sharp rise in U.S. interest rates would occur in the short term.
A more significant rise in U.S. interest rates or a slowdown in economic growth in China could force the bank's economists to revise their forecasts, he said.
The Hong Kong government forecasts GDP growth of 4.7 percent this year.
